statements.quote: The transformer you have been building all this chapter passes every token through every weight: one dense feed-forward block per layer, and that block is the bulk of the model's parameters.
That means the model's **capacity** (how many parameters it stores) and its **compute per token** (how many it actually uses) are the same number — you cannot have one without the other.
**Mixture of Experts (MoE)** breaks that lock.

It lets a model *store* a very large number of parameters while *activating* only a small fraction for each token — so you get the knowledge of a 600-billion-parameter model at the speed and cost of a 30-billion one.

By 2026 this is not a niche trick; it is how most frontier models are built (\cite[Jiang et al., 2024]{mixtral2024}; \cite[DeepSeek-V3, 2024]{deepseekv3tech2024}), and it is the single most important reason the "size of a model" question has quietly become two questions: *total* and *active*.
Recall the per-layer structure from [The Transformer](transformer.php): an attention block, then a feed-forward (FFN) block.

statements.quote: Given a token's hidden state $h$, the router computes a score for each expert and the model keeps only the **top-$k$** (often $k=1$ or $k=2$):
statements.section: The core idea: swap the FFN for a bank of routed experts

statements.quote: The router (a small linear layer) scores all $E$ experts and the token is computed only by the $k$ it selects — here two of four.
statements.section: The core idea: swap the FFN for a bank of routed experts

statements.quote: The idle experts cost memory, not compute, for this token.
statements.section: The core idea: swap the FFN for a bank of routed experts

statements.quote: The router looks trivial — in the original it is a linear projection to $E$ scores plus a learned noise branch — but its *behavior* is the whole story.
statements.section: Routing: a learned sparse switch

statements.quote: In the standard **top-$k$** form, the router computes a softmax over the $E$ experts, keeps the $k$ largest, and renormalizes those $k$ to sum to one; the token's output is the weighted sum of those $k$ experts' outputs.
statements.section: Routing: a learned sparse switch

statements.quote: The router is trained *end-to-end* with the rest of the model, so it learns to send "this kind of token" to the experts that are good at it.
statements.section: Routing: a learned sparse switch

statements.quote: In practice specialization is weaker and more local than the slogan suggests: experts often divide tokens by position, syntax, or surface form rather than by clean domains, and the router's choices are only loosely interpretable (\cite[Xue et al., 2024]{xue2024openmoe}).
statements.section: Routing: a learned sparse switch

statements.quote: The model can therefore afford to be *bad at most things* in any one expert, because each expert only ever sees the slice of tokens that gets routed to it.
statements.section: Routing: a learned sparse switch

statements.quote: A later refinement, used in DeepSeek-V3 (\cite[DeepSeek-V3, 2024]{deepseekv3tech2024}), replaces the softmax-over-all-experts with a **sigmoid** gate: each expert is scored independently, the top-$k$ are chosen, and the selection is not noised; instead a per-expert bias is adjusted during training to keep the load even (\cite[Wang et al., 2024]{wang2024auxfree}).
statements.section: Routing: a learned sparse switch

statements.quote: The difference is subtle but it matters at scale: the sigmoid variant keeps every expert *reachable* for any token, which is exactly what you want when $E$ is in the hundreds.
statements.section: Routing: a learned sparse switch

statements.quote: The deeper point is that routing is a **learned sparse switch**: the model is no longer one function but a family of them, and the router is the part that picks which family member to run — a decision that is itself learned, not designed.
statements.section: Routing: a learned sparse switch

statements.quote: Shazeer's layer is more than a linear gate.
statements.section: Routing: a learned sparse switch

statements.quote: The original router adds Gaussian noise to the logits before the top-$k$ selection (\cite[Shazeer et al., 2017]{shazeer2017moe}), which keeps early training from committing to one expert, and it trains under two pressures: the task loss and an auxiliary loss that penalizes both uneven *importance* (the sum of gate probabilities) and uneven *load* (the number of tokens dispatched).
statements.section: Routing: a learned sparse switch

statements.quote: The top-$k$ itself is non-differentiable, so gradients reach the router only through the selected gate values; the auxiliary terms are what keep that sparse signal from collapsing onto a few experts.
statements.section: Routing: a learned sparse switch

statements.quote: Here is the failure mode that a MoE must fight, and the reason a whole class of training machinery exists.
statements.section: Load balancing: why the experts would otherwise collapse

statements.quote: A router left to itself **collapses**.
statements.section: Load balancing: why the experts would otherwise collapse

statements.quote: Because routing a token to a single expert is "cheaper" in gradient terms than splitting it across several, an unbalanced router drifts until a few experts grab *almost all* the traffic and the rest starve.
statements.section: Load balancing: why the experts would otherwise collapse

statements.quote: The model's effective capacity then silently shrinks back toward a dense model — you built $E$ experts and the router quietly uses two.
statements.section: Load balancing: why the experts would otherwise collapse

statements.quote: GShard (\cite[Lepikhin et al., 2021]{lepikhin2021gshard}; arXiv 2020) is the bridge between the 2017 layer and the trillion-parameter runs.

statements.quote: It scaled a sparse MoE to 600 billion parameters for multilingual translation, used top-2 gating with a hard **expert capacity** — a limit on how many tokens each expert may accept — and added random routing during training so that even lightly scored experts receive gradient.
statements.section: Load balancing: why the experts would otherwise collapse

statements.quote: Just as importantly, it introduced automatic sharding, which lets the experts live on different devices and turns expert parallelism into a compiler problem rather than a hand-built one.

statements.quote: Switch Transformers (\cite[Fedus et al., 2022]{switchtransformers2022}) made the sparse layer simple enough to scale to a trillion parameters.

statements.quote: Its signature change was **top-1 routing** — a single expert per token — which is simpler and faster than top-2 and is enough *if* the experts stay balanced.

statements.quote: The **load-balancing auxiliary loss** it relies on goes back to Shazeer et al. (\cite[Shazeer et al., 2017]{shazeer2017moe}), and Switch keeps it to punish collapse.

statements.section: Shared experts: the part everyone needs, plus the part each token picks

statements.quote: The first is a **shared expert**: one expert is *dense* — every token goes through it — while the remaining experts are *sparse* — routed as usual.
statements.section: Shared experts: the part everyone needs, plus the part each token picks

statements.quote: The shared expert holds the knowledge that *every* token needs (syntax, general language form), and the routed experts hold the *specialized* knowledge (a domain, a rare pattern).
statements.section: Shared experts: the part everyone needs, plus the part each token picks

statements.quote: It is a clean split: "what everyone shares" + "what this token picks." The second idea, **auxiliary-loss-free balancing**, replaces the fixed aux penalty with a *dynamic* router whose bias grows for under-used experts and shrinks for over-used ones, so the routing self-corrects during training rather than being tugged by a separate term — reported to give a stable run at 671 billion parameters with no irrecoverable loss spikes \cite[DeepSeek-V3 (2024)]{deepseekv3tech2024}.
statements.section: Shared experts: the part everyone needs, plus the part each token picks

statements.quote: DeepSeekMoE made the expert bank finer and split off the part every token needs.
statements.section: Shared experts: the part everyone needs, plus the part each token picks

statements.quote: It segments each expert into smaller pieces, so a token can combine several narrow specialists instead of one broad FFN, and it isolates a **shared expert** that every token passes through (\cite[DeepSeekMoE, 2024]{deepseekmoe2024}).
statements.section: Shared experts: the part everyone needs, plus the part each token picks

statements.quote: The shared expert carries common syntax and language structure; the routed experts are free to specialize.
statements.section: Shared experts: the part everyone needs, plus the part each token picks

statements.quote: DeepSeek-V3 keeps this design and adds auxiliary-loss-free balancing, where a per-expert bias — not an extra loss term — is adjusted during training to keep the load even (\cite[Wang et al., 2024]{wang2024auxfree}).

statements.quote: If experts are the point, the engineering question is *where they sit*.
statements.section: Expert parallelism: where the experts live

statements.quote: In **expert parallelism** the $E$ experts are **sharded across devices**: each accelerator holds a different subset of experts, so a 671B model's weights spread over many chips.
statements.section: Expert parallelism: where the experts live

statements.quote: For a given token, the system routes to the devices that hold its $k$ experts, gathers their outputs, and scatters the next token — an **all-to-all** communication pattern in both directions.
statements.section: Expert parallelism: where the experts live

statements.quote: This is why MoE is famously cheap to *train* per active parameter but awkward to *serve*: the all-to-all is a synchronous, latency-sensitive step, and a request can only move on once every device holding one of its experts has answered.
statements.section: Expert parallelism: where the experts live

statements.quote: The training side of this is [Training Infrastructure](training_infrastructure.php); the serving side is [Inference vs Training](inference_vs_training.php).
statements.section: Expert parallelism: where the experts live

statements.quote: The conceptual point is that *routing* (which expert) and *parallelism* (which device) are separate decisions that compose — the router decides the logic, the parallelism decides the physics.
